title: Canada joins NATO Innovation Fund with contribution of about $100-million
html:
The NATO Innovation Fund announced Saturday that Canada had officially become the 25th allied country to back it.Virginia Mayo/The Associated Press

Canada is committing approximately $100-million to joining the NATO Innovation Fund, opening up the $1.7-billion-plus multinational venture capital pool to domestic companies working on defence and security technologies.

In July, The Globe and Mail reported that the final hurdle to Canada joining was approval of its application by the 24 countries already participating in the fund. On Saturday, the NIF announced Canada had officially become the 25th allied country to back it, with a contribution that will be managed by the Business Development Bank of Canada.

The fund’s president, Ari Jonsson, said Canada’s application was met with unanimous approval.

“In terms of technologies that can fill technology gaps for NATO, Canada has a vibrant ecosystem,” he told The Globe.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said Canada’s contribution to the fund will count toward the country meeting its commitment as a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to spend 5 per cent of gross domestic product on defence by 2035.

“Canada’s got incredible world-class technologies, and increasingly, those technologies are being harnessed, directed and deployed in the direction of defence materiel needs,” he said in an interview. “So we really recognize this is a good time to move forward and execute.”

The NIF is a stand-alone venture capital fund that NATO founded in 2022, although the alliance itself has not invested in it financially – nor is it involved in any of its decision-making.

Rather, the capital for the fund comes from its participating allies. Canada’s commitment just upped the total – though it’s been a long time coming.

The country signed off on the creation of the NIF four years ago and Ottawa even set aside $107-million over 20 years in 2024 to participate in the venture, but ultimately did not join it. Then, in June, in response to questions from The Globe, the Department of National Defence said Canada was “actively considering options” to join the fund and that the original $107-million pot was still available.

On Saturday, Ottawa finally followed through.

The country’s membership in the NIF opens up the Canadian market to the fund’s investors, as well as bringing Canadians into the existing network of entrepreneurs, investors and governments with knowledge of how to finance the growing defence sector.

It will also provide insight into the Canadian ecosystem for those already in the network.

“The first objective of Canada joining NIF is to expose our innovators to the NATO alliance, but also to expose NIF to our Canadian innovators,” Isabelle Hudon, president of BDC, told The Globe.

The NIF’s first subfund, established in 2023, focuses on investing in early-stage startups working on technologies that strengthen defence, security and resilience. It can also invest in other funds with similar mandates.

Mr. Jonsson said he expects to launch more subfunds in line with NATO’s technological demands, but does not have a concrete plan or timeline yet.

“We’re all aware that the need is great, and the need is near in time, and that is really our responsibility, to respond to those needs. That’s what will drive our future subfund developments,” he said.

Earlier this year, German space company Isar Aerospace and Finnish airship maker Kelluu, both NIF portfolio companies, began establishing a presence in Canada. The NIF aims to cultivate these types of activities, said Amalia Kontesi, chief communications and marketing officer for the fund.

“Our aspiration is to serve as a bridge between the Canadian ecosystem and the European ecosystem,” she said.

The NIF is headquartered in the Netherlands, domiciled in Luxembourg and has regional offices in Poland and Britain. Its 25 participating allies include Germany, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Greece and Norway.

Next year, Mr. Jonsson said, NIF plans to have staff in Canada, and the fund has already begun forming an idea of where they should be based and travel to, informed by discussions with BDC and other Canadian funds.
summary: Membership opens up the $1.7-billion-plus multinational venture capital pool to Canadian companies
